title: Floating-Point Representation and Precision
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter is about how a computer stores the numbers it computes with, and why that storage scheme — not any error in your code — is responsible for surprises like `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`. It covers integer representations, the IEEE floating-point format used for real numbers, and the practical consequences: when you may and may not test numbers for equality, and how naive arithmetic can silently destroy precision. It assumes you can read Python/numpy code and are comfortable with binary and scientific notation; it does not assume any numerical-analysis background, since building the intuition for why computer arithmetic is not the arithmetic of the real numbers is the point of the chapter. ## Bits, bytes, and integers Everything in computer memory or on disk is stored as bits — switches that are either on or off — so everything is ultimately a number in base 2. Eight bits make a byte, and since a byte has $2^8 = 256$ possible values, it is often written more compactly as two base-16 (hexadecimal) digits, such as `3e` or `a0`. A file format is nothing more than a convention for interpreting the bytes in a file; the same bit pattern is a character, an integer, or a fraction of a real number depending on which convention is applied to it. Integers are the simplest case. With two bytes (16 bits) you can encode an *unsigned* integer from $0$ to $2^{16}-1 = 65535$. To also store negative numbers, the natural idea is to spend one bit on a sign, leaving $2^{15}-1 = 32767$ in magnitude, i.e. a range of $-32767$ to $32767$. In practice, negative integers are not stored simply as a sign bit plus a magnitude — they use a different binary encoding chosen specifically to make arithmetic circuitry simple. (As a way to get a feel for this, try adding the 64-bit binary representations of $-1$ and $1$ bit by bit — the result comes out right in an very simple way.) Fixed-width integers are not closed under arithmetic: multiplying two computer integers can produce a result too large to store, which **overflows** silently. A 32-bit integer holds values up to $2^{31}-1 = 2147483647$ (with $2\cdot 2^{31} = 2^{32} = (2^8)^4$, consistent with 4 bytes of 8 bits each); square a modest six-digit number like $3423333$ as a 32-bit integer and you overflow, while the same multiplication in 64 bits is fine — until the inputs are themselves large enough that a 64-bit product overflows too, which numpy will not warn you about. Python's own `int` type is arbitrary-precision and never overflows this way, but it costs more memory than a fixed-width numpy integer and, used in bulk (as a list of ordinary Python ints rather than a numpy array), gives up the efficient array-based computation that fixed-width, contiguous storage makes possible. So the choice of integer type is a real trade-off between exactness, memory, and speed — not a detail to default your way past. ## Floating-point representation Real numbers ("floating points") are stored as an *approximation* — an extremely precise one, but an approximation. If you represented the earth–sun distance as a double, the error would be around a millimeter; the trouble comes when a calculation produces a very small or very large number, and especially when you ask whether two numbers are *equal*. ### Why "floating" The natural way to store a real number in a fixed number of digits is scientific notation: $$\pm d_0.d_1 d_2 \ldots d_p \times b^e$$ where $b$ is the base, $e$ (the *exponent*) is an integer, and $d = d_1 d_2 \ldots d_p$ (the *mantissa*) has digits $d_i \in \{0, \ldots, b-1\}$. The decimal point "floats" to wherever the exponent puts it, which is what lets a fixed number of digits represent both very large and very small magnitudes while keeping the same relative precision throughout. Fixing the decimal point instead would cost you precision. With three base-10 digits and a floating point, $0.12 \times 0.12 = 0.0144$ is stored as $(1.20\times10^{-1})\times(1.20\times10^{-1}) = 1.44\times10^{-2}$ — exact to three significant digits. Fix the decimal point at three places after it and you get $0.120 \times 0.120 = 0.014$, losing a digit of accuracy (and you could not represent anything larger than $0.99$ at all). ### The IEEE double Designing this scheme on a computer, using base 2, means choosing how many bits to spend on the exponent (how large or small a magnitude you can reach) versus the mantissa (how much precision you get). The standard choice for a *double* (8 bytes = 64 bits) is: $$(-1)^S \times 1.d \times 2^{e-1023} = (-1)^S \times 1.d_1 d_2 \ldots d_{52} \times 2^{e-1023}$$ with the number split into a sign bit $S$, an 11-bit exponent field $e$ (so $2^{11}=2048$ possible values), and $p = 64 - 1 - 11 = 52$ mantissa bits $d$. The leading `1.` before the mantissa is always present and does not need to be stored — it is the *hidden bit*. Requiring it also *normalizes* the representation, giving every number a single, unique encoding rather than several equivalent ones (e.g. $1 = 1.0\times2^0 = 0.1\times2^1 = 0.01\times2^2$, of which only the first is allowed). Subtracting the bias, $1023$, from the stored exponent field takes the place of a separate sign bit for the exponent. As a worked example, the bit pattern for $5.25$ has exponent field $10000000001_2 = 1025$, and mantissa $0101\ldots$, giving $$1.0101 \times 2^{1025-1023} = \left(1\times2^2 + 0\times2^1 + 1\times2^0 + 0\times2^{-1} + 1\times2^{-2}\right) = 4 + 1 + 0.25 = 5.25.$$ Not every real number lands exactly on one of these bit patterns. $0.5 = 1.0\times2^{-1}$ is exact, but $0.1$ is not representable exactly in base 2 for the same reason $1/3$ is not representable exactly in base 10 — no finite number of base-2 digits sums to it. Doubles are the default in most numerical work, but a 4-byte *single precision* float also exists (the original, older standard) and is now used again on GPUs for speed and reduced memory: a numpy array of `float32` uses half the memory of the same array in `float64`, and `float16` less still. ## Machine epsilon and how much precision you actually have *Machine epsilon* is the smallest float $x$ such that $1 + x \neq 1$ in computer arithmetic — the smallest possible relative change you can register near $1$. It has an equivalent description in terms of spacing: the next representable double above $1 = 1.00\ldots0\times2^0$ is $1.00\ldots01\times2^0$, and the gap between them is $$\epsilon = 0\times2^0 + 0\times2^{-1} + \cdots + 0\times2^{-51} + 1\times2^{-52} = 2^{-52} \approx 2.2\times10^{-16}.$$ Single precision, with far fewer mantissa bits, has a correspondingly much larger machine epsilon — much less precision per number. This spacing scales with magnitude: machine epsilon gives the *absolute* spacing of numbers near 1, but the *relative* spacing everywhere, since the next representable number above any $x$ is $(1+\epsilon)x$, so the relative spacing is $$\frac{(1+\epsilon)x - x}{x} = \epsilon$$ regardless of $x$'s magnitude. That means the *absolute* error in representing a number of magnitude $x$ is about $x\epsilon$: at $x = 10^6$, the absolute error is about $2\times10^{-10}$, so you have about 16 significant (not decimal) digits of accuracy whether $x$ is tiny or huge — because moving the exponent $e$ rescales which power of 2 the least-significant mantissa bit (the *ulp*, unit in the last place) corresponds to, but not how many significant bits you have. With $p=52$ mantissa bits, $2^{52} \approx 0.5\times10^{16}$ distinct values are representable per octave, which is where "about 16 significant digits" comes from directly. One useful consequence: an integer-valued number stored as a double is exact as long as its absolute value is less than $2^{53}$ — one bit more than the 52 stored mantissa bits, thanks to the hidden leading 1. Past that, the spacing between representable doubles grows past 1 (at $2^{53}$ the spacing is already $2$, at $2^{54}$ it is $4$, and so on), so consecutive integers start to be unrepresentable. ## Overflow and underflow The exponent field has $2^{11} = 2048$ possible values, so the largest exponent gives a magnitude of about $2^{1024}$, and $$\log_{10} 2^{1024} = \frac{1024}{\log_2 10} \approx \frac{1024}{3.32} \approx 308,$$ so doubles overflow somewhere around $10^{308}$ (the very top of the exponent range is reserved so that infinity has a representation) and underflow — silently, with no warning — somewhere around $10^{-308}$. There is a subtlety just past that boundary: numbers with magnitude between roughly $10^{-309}$ and $10^{-323}$ can still be represented even though the normal exponent range alone would suggest the smallest representable magnitude is about $2^{-1023}\approx10^{-308}$ — a detail left as an exercise to investigate rather than derived here. Integers behave differently under overflow than floats do in one respect worth noting: whereas a double simply loses precision as it grows and eventually overflows around $10^{308}$, a fixed-width integer can overflow at a comparatively tiny value (a 64-bit integer overflows well before $2^{65}$), even though a double of the same magnitude would still be represented without issue — just not exactly. ## Why computer arithmetic is not real-number arithmetic Because both the range and the precision are finite, computer arithmetic on floats fails two properties you take for granted with real numbers: it is not closed (multiplying two representable floats can overflow to something unrepresentable), and it is not associative or distributive: $(a+b)+c$ need not equal $a+(b+c)$, and $a(b+c)$ need not equal $ab+ac$, purely because of the order in which rounding happens. Multiplying `val1*val2*val3` and `val3*val2*val1` for `val1, val2, val3 = 0.1, 0.31, 0.57` can produce two different floating-point results, even though multiplication of real numbers is commutative. Integer arithmetic, by contrast, is fast and exact (subject to overflow); floating-point arithmetic is slower and only approximate. Because of that cost, a *flop* (floating-point operation — one multiplication or division combined with one addition or subtraction) is the standard unit for how much numerical work a calculation does. ## Comparing floating-point numbers The practical rule that follows directly from all of this: never test `x == y` on floats unless 1. `x` and `y` are represented as integers, 2. they are integer-valued but stored as doubles small enough to be exact (below $2^{53}$ in magnitude), or 3. they were computed in exactly the same way (`0.4 - 0.3 == 0.4 - 0.3` is `True`, but `0.1 == 0.4 - 0.3` is not, even though both sides are "the same number" mathematically). The same caution applies to testing `x == 0` and to `<`/`>` comparisons: `x[x < 0]` finds values that are *numerically* less than zero, which is not always the same set as the values that are *mathematically* less than zero. A workable notion of approximate equality falls directly out of the definition of machine epsilon: declare $a$ and $b$ equal if their relative spacing is below machine epsilon (or, to be safe, a small multiple of it), $$|a - b| < \epsilon \, |a+b|,$$ using that the absolute spacing at magnitude $x$ is $x\epsilon$. One case where exact `==` testing on floats *is* safe: an unusual integer used as a sentinel for missing data (e.g. `-9999`). Because integers of that magnitude are stored exactly as doubles, `x[x == -9999] = np.nan` is fine — though reading the column in as an integer or string type and checking before converting to float is the fully careful version. ## Catastrophic cancellation Subtracting two large numbers that are nearly equal (or adding numbers of similar magnitude and opposite sign) throws away most of your precision, because the *absolute* error in each of the original numbers is already large relative to the difference you're trying to compute. $$123456781234.56 - 123456781234.00$$ Each operand has magnitude $x \approx 10^{11}$, so each carries an absolute error of about $\epsilon x \approx 2.2\times10^{-16}\times10^{11} \approx 10^{-5}$. The true difference is close to $1$, so you might expect an answer accurate to machine epsilon — but the error that matters is the error already present in the *inputs*, not in the subtraction itself, and it swamps everything past about the fifth significant digit of the result. This loss of significant digits to a subtraction of near-equal quantities is *catastrophic cancellation*: most of what remains in the result is rounding error, because the genuine significant digits cancelled against each other. The same thing happens with small numbers. Subtracting $x = 0.000000000000123412341234$ and $y = 0.000000000000123412340000$ should give exactly $0.000000000000000000001234$, but the computed difference is accurate only to about 28 decimal places rather than the 36 you would hope for (16 significant digits plus the 20 leading zeros) — 8 digits are lost to cancellation, exactly matching the position (the 13th significant digit) at which $x$ and $y$ first differ. This is not a corner case: it shows up in ordinary statistical computation. The textbook formula for a sample variance, $$s^2 = \sum_i x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2,$$ computed this way can lose essentially all of its accuracy once the $x_i$ are shifted to have a large mean — subtracting two large, nearly-equal sums of squares — even though the mathematically equivalent, mean-centered form $\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2$ gives the right answer on the same data. The general principle is to subtract off a value close in magnitude to what you're working with (here, $\bar x$) before doing arithmetic that would otherwise cancel large digits; the same idea rescues the quadratic formula when its two forms are compared for a root near zero (see Gentle, p. 101, for the worked case — not reproduced here). ## Mixing magnitudes, and the order of summation A related but distinct problem: adding or subtracting numbers of very different magnitude. The result can only be as precise as the *larger* number allows, since that is the number whose absolute precision limits the sum. Subtracting a small correction from a number of magnitude $10^{11}$ (whose absolute error is already around $10^{-5}$) has literally no effect once the correction is smaller than $10^{-5}$ — the same phenomenon as computing $1 + 10^{-16}$ and getting back exactly $1$. This has a direct implication for how you sum a long list of numbers of similar-ish magnitude: adding them in increasing order (so each addition combines numbers as close in size as possible for as long as possible) preserves more precision than adding in an arbitrary order. If all the numbers are of genuinely similar size, even that eventually fails, because the running partial sum grows much larger than each new term; the fix there is to sum in a tree-like fashion, so that every individual addition combines two partial sums of comparable size rather than one huge sum and one small term. ## Staying on the log scale The *range* problem (as opposed to the precision problem above) shows up whenever you multiply or divide many numbers, especially many large or small ones: the product can overflow or underflow well before any individual factor would. **Never take the product of many large or small numbers directly.** Instead compute on the log scale and exponentiate only at the very end, using $$\prod_i x_i \Big/ \prod_j y_j = \exp\left(\sum_i \log x_i - \sum_j \log y_j\right),$$ and often you can avoid exponentiating at all — for instance when the final goal is to maximize a log-likelihood. Two situations where this matters in statistical computing: - **Multiclass logistic regression.** The class probabilities are $$p_j = \Pr(y=j) = \frac{\exp(x\beta_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^K \exp(x\beta_k)} = \frac{\exp(z_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^K \exp(z_k)}, \qquad z_k = x\beta_k.$$ If the $z_k$ are large in magnitude (positive or negative), evaluating this directly overflows or underflows the exponentials before you ever get to divide. - **Averaging a predictive density over posterior draws**, as in Bayesian model comparison: $$f(y^*\mid y,x) = \int f(y^*\mid y,x,\theta)\,\pi(\theta\mid y,x)\,d\theta \approx \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i^*\mid x,\theta_j) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \log f(y_i^*\mid x,\theta_j)\right) \equiv \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \exp(v_j).$$ Each $v_j$ is a sum of $n$ log-likelihood terms and can easily be something like $-1000$, so $e^{v_j}$ underflows to exactly $0$ long before you can average it. You cannot exponentiate each $v_j$ individually and then sum; this "log sum of exponentials" problem, and its standard resolution, is known as the **log-sum-exp trick**. ## Numerical loss of positive-definiteness Numerical range and precision limits also bite in linear algebra. A covariance or correlation matrix that is *mathematically* positive definite — every eigenvalue strictly positive — can come out with small negative eigenvalues when computed numerically. A squared-exponential correlation matrix built from pairwise distances (mathematically positive definite for any set of points) is a standard example where the smallest numerical eigenvalues can be negative once you actually compute them, purely from the accumulation of rounding error in the eigenvalue computation. ## Exercises These are discussion questions posed during the lecture itself, not a separate problem set; they are reproduced here as questions to work through, not answered. 1. Given a fixed total number of bits for a floating-point number, what is the trade-off between spending more of them on the mantissa $d$ versus more of them on the exponent $e$? 2. Why can integer-valued numbers be stored exactly as a double precisely up to $2^{53}$ in absolute value? Work out, in terms of the $(S, d, e)$ representation, which integers admit an exact base-2 expansion of this form. 3. In the multiclass logistic regression setup above, $p_j = \exp(z_j)/\sum_k \exp(z_k)$: if the $z_k$ are large in magnitude, how should the expression be re-written so that it can actually be evaluated? (Hint: multiply by $c/c$ for a well-chosen constant $c$.) 4. In the predictive-density calculation above, why is it natural to work with the *log* conditional predictive density rather than the density itself? Given an estimate on the log scale, $\log f(y^*\mid y,x) \approx \log\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \exp(v_j)$, with some $v_j$ as extreme as $-1000$, how do you evaluate the right-hand side without any individual term underflowing to zero? 5. (Noted in the lecture as a possible extra-credit problem, not solved there.) Explain how numbers with magnitude between about $10^{-309}$ and $10^{-323}$ can still be represented as doubles, even though the ordinary exponent range would suggest that $2^{-1023}\approx10^{-308}$ is the smallest representable magnitude. ## Sources This chapter is drawn entirely from the "1. Basic representations" / "2. Floating point basics" / "3. Implications for calculations and comparisons" sequence of Unit 8 ("Numbers") of UC Berkeley's STAT 243, in the two most recent offerings supplied: - `berkeley-stat243/fall-2024/units/unit8-numbers.qmd`, split as `01-1-basic-representations.md`, `02-2-floating-point-basics.md`, and `03-3-implications-for-calculations-and-comparisons.md`. - `berkeley-stat243/fall-2025/units/unit8-numbers.qmd`, split the same way. The two offerings are essentially the same lecture; the 2025 version corrects a small bug in the `approx_equal` code example (it calls the function on the variables it just defined, `x` and `y`, where the 2024 version accidentally reused stale variables `a` and `b`) and is otherwise identical in content and worked examples. Both cite Gentle, *Computational Statistics*, ch. 2 (including the quadratic-formula cancellation example on p. 101, referenced but not reproduced in either source), Monahan, ch. 2, for further detail, and ; none of these external references were supplied as input and so are named here without being drawn on further. The `gmpy2`-based higher-precision arithmetic example mentioned at the end of the source material is a pointer to a library, not a topic developed in the lecture, and is likewise not covered here. A third input file group was also supplied with this task — `stat243-fall-2021/units/unit8-bigData/` (preparatory notes, Hadoop/MapReduce/Spark/Dask, and databases). That material is on a different topic entirely (large-scale data tools, not number representation) and belongs to a different unit of the course: in the fall-2021 offering, the numbers material lived in `unit6-numbers.md` rather than in unit 8, and the two course iterations only coincide on the unit *number* "8", not on its content, because the units were renumbered between 2021 and 2024. It is not used in this chapter.
